messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]     MRN: [REDACTED]     DOB: [REDACTED]     Admission Date: [REDACTED]     Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted to the emergency department with complaints of chest pain, shortness of breath, and a productive cough. Upon examination, the patient was found to have tachycardia and tachypnea. Laboratory findings revealed leukocytosis with elevated C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. CT chest showed left lower lobe pneumonia and a large pericardial effusion. The patient received appropriate treatment for pneumonia and underwent transthoracic echocardiogram to further characterize the effusion as moderate circumferential pericardial effusion.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: [diagnosis section withheld]
DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
Upon consultation with the patient’s psychiatrist, clozapine was stopped, which was thought to be the cause for the non-resolving pericardial effusion. Following the discontinuation of the drug, there was a gradual improvement in the respiratory status. The patient was discontinued from clozapine and discharged to home in stable and improved condition.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient is advised to follow up with their primary care provider for future management of high cholesterol and assistance with smoking cessation.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
None prescribed at this time.

FOLLOW-UP STUDIES:
Transthoracic echocardiogram to be repeated for further evaluation in one year.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
Stable and improved.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
1. The condition chiefly responsible for this admission is the clozapine-induced, non-resolving pericardial effusion: it drove the echo work-up and the decision to stop clozapine, and the pneumonia was treated alongside it.
2. It belongs to chapter I, and drug-induced effusion maps to "other diseases of pericardium" (category I31).
3. I30 (acute pericarditis) is a close alternative given the chest pain and raised inflammatory markers, and pneumonia (J18) is possible, so this choice is uncertain.

CODE: I31
